extracted.intended_audience: general readers of popular science / natural history enthusiasts
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes criteria, experimental methods, and observational evidence used to assess cognitive and social behaviors in ants (e.g., direction sense, communication, memory, recognition, emotions, nursing, husbandry, slavery, warfare). Useful as a checklist of phenomena and the types of experiments/observations that demonstrate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of Direction
rubrics_metrics.description: Ants possess an unaccountable sense of direction enabling them to find their way independently of landmarks; this sense apparently registers lateral changes of direction made during outward journeys rather than velocity along the line of progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental demonstrations (Sir John Lubbock): 1) hat-box on a pivot with holes — when box rotated after an ant entered, the ant turned with the box, retaining her direction; 2) white paper disk moved under an ant conveying it beyond her intended point — the ant continued to the far edge (appearing surprised). These show ants track orientation via accumulated directional changes; design anti-patterns: moving the substrate without tracking lateral turns would misinterpret results; scoring/evidence: consistent directional corrections across manipulations indicate internal registration of turns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers of Communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Ants can communicate information to one another by a system of signs or signals, sufficient to recruit nestmates to food/larvae and to indicate which source is richer, though not to describe precise locality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observational examples: Hague's mantel-shelf vase — killing a few ants on a trail caused approaching ants to turn away and eliminate the traffic to that vase until reappearance after days; Sir John Lubbock's controlled experiment with three tapes to glass vessels (one with many larvae, one with few, one empty): ants with access to numerous larvae recruited far more helpers (257 friends in 47.5 hours vs. 82 in 53 hours), indicating definite communication about where larger stores are. Follow-up showed ants cannot give precise guidance: when returning ants were carried to larvae and allowed only to return with a larva, recruited ants wandered and largely failed to find the resource (only 5 of 120 found it by chance). Guidance: use controlled placement, replacement of resources to avoid depletion, and capture/immobilization manipulations to test whether recruits follow chemical trails, guidance behaviors, or spatial instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Ants remember the way to stores of food or larvae and will return repeatedly; memory follows similar properties to general memory — formed by repetition and liable to decay over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Lubbock's need to repeat lessons for long/unusual routes; Belt's leaf-cutting ants possibly remembering nest site for twelve months after forced migration (carbolic acid treatment), and Karl Vogt's report of ants' repeated seasonal visits to a syrup vessel 600 metres away. Guidance: demonstrate memory by showing repeat visits after intervals, control for simple trail scent cues versus true long-term retention (e.g., removal of pheromone trails, relocation experiments), and consider alternative accidental re-discovery hypotheses when distances are large.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (Nestmate/Colony Recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: All ants of the same community recognize one another as friends; ants introduced from other nests—even of the same species—are identified as foreigners and attacked. Recognition persists over long separations and may reflect blood-relationship or colony-specific cues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key experiments: Huber — ants removed and absent for four months still recognized; Lubbock — larvae removed, raised away, then returned as adults were still accepted; division of a nest before queens were gravid produced groups which, seven months later, reciprocally accepted young transferred between divisions, indicating recognition not based on individual appearance or learned pass-words but possibly on lineage. Larger-scale cases: 'nations' of nests (Forel) and 'ant towns' (McCook) with hundreds/thousands of nests all recognizing each other. Guidance: test recognition by long separations, raising individuals from larval stage away from colony, and cross-transfers between divisions; consider slave-making ants' exceptions (Forel) where slave identity recognition differs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotions (Affection, Sympathy, Hatred)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ants display aggressive traits (pugnacity, valor, rapacity) and, in some species, evidence of tender emotions (sympathy, affection); species differ markedly in responsiveness to injured or imprisoned companions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixed observations: Lubbock found many species apparently deficient in affection/sympathy (burying experiments where passing ants did not free imprisoned nestmates); in some species (Formica rufescens) ants ignored both friends and strangers; counter-evidence shows sympathy: injured or antennaless ants being examined, carried gently into nest; Moggridge saw ants rescue and revive apparently dead individuals by dipping them in water; Belt observed Eciton humata coordinating rescues and digging out buried comrades. Guidance: species-level variation matters — design species-specific tests (burying, injuring, visible distress) and observe for coordinated rescue behavior, carrying of sick to nest, or neglect; beware of overgeneralizing from one species to Formicidae as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nursing and Care of Brood
rubrics_metrics.description: Workers nurse eggs, larvae, and pupae with attentive behaviors (licking eggs to promote growth, moving brood relative to heat/moisture, feeding larvae by mouth-to-mouth, assisting emergence from cocoons), and educate young workers to tasks and recognition of friends/enemies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptions: eggs require licking to develop; workers move eggs/larvae to appropriate nest microclimates; feeding by mouth contact; workers bite pupal cases to free young and remove the membranous 'shirt'; young are led about and taught duties, and avoid fighting when nest attacked (they remove pupae). Forel's experiment with mixing young uneducated ants of hostile species showed they would tend pupae together and not quarrel until maturity, indicating acquired components to species hostility. Guidance: to demonstrate nursing and learning, observe brood-tending behaviors, thermohygro-regulation moves, feeding interactions, and experiments that test innate versus learned hostility (raising young with heterospecific pupae).

rubrics_metrics.name: Keeping Aphides and Other Insect 'Husbandry'
rubrics_metrics.description: Many ants keep aphides, gall-insects, cocci, and even Lycaena caterpillars as 'cows' to harvest sweet secretions, collecting eggs, tending young, constructing enclosures and milking aphids by stroking them with antennae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable variations: Huber's observations of collecting and tending aphid eggs; Lasius flavus case (Lubbock) where aphid eggs are kept in the nest over winter and then placed on host plants in spring (a form of prudential husbandry); Nottebohm's report of ants replanting aphid colonies on a tree after original colonies were destroyed. Where multiple tended insects co-occur, ants keep them in separate chambers/stalls (McCook). Guidance: document egg-collection, stabling behavior (clay walls, door sizes), 'milking' interactions, seasonal translocation of eggs, and controlled removal/replanting experiments to show intentional maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slavery (Slave-making Behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain ant species conduct slave raids: they attack nests of other species, carry off pupae to hatch as slaves, and in some species rely almost entirely on slaves for brood care and feeding; the role division between masters and slaves varies by species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms and variation: P. Huber's Formica rufescens enslaving F. fusca pupae—young slaves integrate and work; JF. sanguinea keeps comparatively few household slaves while masters perform outdoor work; F. rufescens delegates most tasks to slaves and masters are unable to feed themselves without slaves (mouth structure adaptations). Lespes sugar experiment: masters reminded slaves to feed them by pulling legs; slaves serve under threat of punishment. Other cases: Audubon's report of leaf-bugs used as slaves in Brazil assisting in carrying leaves, then kept and fed scantily. Guidance: evidence includes observation of raids, transport of pupae, functional dependence (masters failing to feed themselves), and controlled feeding/punishment observations; examine morphological adaptations that indicate dependence on slaves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wars and Organized Raiding
rubrics_metrics.description: Slave-making and marauding species organize large-scale, strategic raids with scouts, columns, and coordinated marching to plunder other nests, often capturing thousands of pupae in a season.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed patterns (Lespes, Forel): scouts explore and identify targets, return to guide the host army; columns of 1–2 thousand individuals march in order for extended periods (e.g., 5 metres long, 50 cm wide, 1 m/min pace), engage in fierce battles, and, if successful, carry off pupae back along the same scented track. Forel recorded a colony sending 44 expeditions in 30 days with 28 successes; average booty ~1000 pupae per successful expedition (estimated seasonal capture ~40,000 pupae). Guidance: quantify expedition frequency/success, measure column dimensions and pace, document scouting behavior and return guidance, and trace pheromone trail use (returning on same track). Use careful counts to estimate colony-level impacts.
